101:### Status codes
102-
103-Streaming page responses begin with a `200` status code.
104-
105-The initial response headers set the status for the rest of the response. Next.js can then stream redirects and HTTP access fallbacks with [`redirect`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect), [`notFound`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found), [`forbidden`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/forbidden), or [`unauthorized`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/unauthorized).
106-
107-For example, when a 404 page is streamed to the client, Next.js includes a `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` tag in the streamed HTML. This prevents search engines from indexing that URL even if the HTTP status is 200. See Google’s guidance on the [`robots` meta tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag).
108-
109-Some crawlers may label these responses as “soft 404s”. The `noindex` tag keeps them out of search results.
110-
111-Run the corresponding check before the response body streams to return a `404`, `403`, or `401` status for compliance or analytics.
112-
113-For a `404`, you can check the slug in [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy), then rewrite it to a not-found route or [return a `404` response](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#producing-a-response). Keep Proxy checks fast, and avoid fetching full content there.
114-
115-<details>
116-<summary>When is the response body streamed?</summary>
117-
118-The response body starts streaming when a Suspense fallback renders (for example, a `loading.tsx`) or when a Server Component suspends under a `<Suspense>` boundary. Calling `notFound()`, `forbidden()`, or `unauthorized()` before this point preserves its `404`, `403`, or `401` status.
119-
120-Starting the stream sends the response headers and fixes the status code.
121-
122-</details>
123-
124-### Browser limits
125-
126-[Some browsers](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=252413) buffer a streaming response. You may not see the streamed response until the response exceeds 1024 bytes. This typically only affects “hello world” applications, but not real applications.

events.content:
The `/admin` page is in place and works. I ran a production build and requested `/admin` with curl: it returned **HTTP 403** and showed the custom error page, with the `noindex` tag Next.js adds. The mock session in `app/lib/auth.ts` is a non-admin user, so that's the expected result.

**What I changed**

- **`next.config.ts`**: turned on `experimental.authInterrupts`. This version of Next.js requires that setting before `forbidden()` and `forbidden.tsx` will work.
- **`app/admin/page.tsx`**: the page calls the existing `verifyAdmin()` from `app/lib/auth.ts` and calls `forbidden()` from `next/navigation` if the user isn't an admin. Admins see "Admin Dashboard" with a welcome message using their name.
- **`app/forbidden.tsx`**: a styled, centred 403 card with "Access forbidden", a short explanation and a "Return home" link. It's at the root of `app/`, so any route that calls `forbidden()` later will use the same page.

**Two things to know**

- **Don't add a `loading.tsx` or `<Suspense>` around the check in `/admin`.** Once the page starts streaming, the status code is already sent as 200. The error page would still appear, but the real 403 would be lost. I left a comment in the page saying this.
- **The build currently treats `/admin` as a static page**, because the mock `getSession()` doesn't read cookies or headers. When you replace it with real session lookup (for example via `cookies()`), the page will be checked on each request automatically. To check the admin view now, change `role: 'user'` to `'admin'` in `app/lib/auth.ts`.

I deleted the files the test build generated (`.next/`, `next-env.d.ts`) and undid the change the build made to `tsconfig.json`. Nothing is committed.

- **`app/admin/page.tsx`**: the page calls the existing `verifyAdmin()` from `app/lib/auth.ts` and calls `forbidden()` from `next/navigation` if the user isn't an admin. Admins see "Admin Dashboard" with a welcome message using their name.
- **`app/forbidden.tsx`**: a styled, centred 403 card with "Access forbidden", a short explanation and a "Return home" link. It's at the root of `app/`, so any route that calls `forbidden()` later will use the same page.
